name: Auburn
headline: Auburn: a south King County city shaped by the Green and White rivers.
lede: Auburn sits in the valley where SR 167 and SR 18 meet, with Lea Hill, West Hill and Lakeland Hills rising around it and a small part reaching into Pierce County. This guide covers getting around, parks and rivers, schools, everyday errands, housing and neighborhoods, and what’s nearby, with a source for every fact.

Mostly King County. A small part at the south end, where Lakeland Hills straddles the county line, is in Pierce County. Auburn voted in 1997 to annex portions of Pierce County

The Green and White rivers shaped the city’s history; Mud Mountain Dam and Howard A. Hanson Dam ended the flooding that had held back growth
SR 167 (the Valley Freeway) and SR 18 meet in Auburn; SR 164 runs east from town

notes: Land area differs by source: the Census Bureau gives 29.58 square miles of land (2020), while Wikipedia’s infobox gives 29.824. This guide uses the Census figure.
Census QuickFacts showed a July 1, 2025 population estimate of 86,301 and 2020–2024 survey figures when checked; Wikipedia lists a 2024 estimate of 85,513. This guide uses the Census figures.

Sounder travel time to Seattle differs: Wikipedia’s Auburn article says about 30 minutes to downtown Seattle, while the Auburn station article says approximately 35 minutes to King Street Station. This guide uses the station article.

The new Sound Transit garage: Wikipedia says 500 stalls, first expected by 2024 and delayed to 2027. Sound Transit’s project page says construction continues and completion is expected by 2027, but it does not give a stall count, so the guide does not state one.

School districts need a closer look. Wikipedia’s Auburn article says the Pierce County part of Auburn is served by the Dieringer School District, but the Auburn School District lists Lake Tapps among the communities it serves and has a Lakeland Hills Elementary. The Dieringer boundary map is a PDF that was not read. Kent and Federal Way service in northern Auburn comes from Wikipedia only.

Wikipedia’s Auburn School District article is internally inconsistent (14 elementary schools in its summary, 16 in its list). The district’s own page says 16 elementary, 4 middle and 4 high schools, and 17,125 K–12 students; this guide uses the district figures.

The City’s parks page gives two trail figures, “over 20 linear miles” and “over 26 miles of trails.” The Game Farm Park page names both the Stuck River and the White River as nearby; the Environmental Park page gives the boardwalk as 1,200 feet and as a quarter mile. This guide uses the less contested figures.
The farmers market details come from a City bulletin for the 2025 season (Sundays through September 14). The 2026 season was not checked.
Pierce Transit route 497 and the Metro routes are listed as Wikipedia states them; routes change often, so confirm with King County Metro, Pierce Transit or Sound Transit.

chapters.title: Getting around and commutes
chapters.intro: Auburn sits where SR 167 and SR 18 meet, with Sounder trains and regional buses at a downtown station. Census figures put the mean travel time to work for Auburn residents at 30.5 minutes (2020–2024).
items: SR 167 runs past The Outlet Collection, along Mill Creek and the Interurban Trail west of downtown, then past Emerald Downs and the airport before crossing the Green River into Kent. It continues north to Renton and south to I-5 in Tacoma.
The northbound HOT lane begins in Auburn and the southbound lane ends in Pacific. Solo drivers pay a variable toll of $1 to $15.
A mostly four-lane freeway that meets SR 167 in Auburn, runs west to I-5 and SR 99 in Federal Way, and east through Covington and Maple Valley to I-90 near Snoqualmie.

Auburn station at 23 A Street Southwest has 13 weekday Sounder S Line round trips, north to Seattle’s King Street Station in approximately 35 minutes and south to Tacoma Dome or Lakewood. It has 633 parking spaces, 520 of them in a six-story garage.
Sound Transit is building a new garage at 1st Street Northwest, along with walking, biking and bus access improvements. The project is expected to be complete by 2027.

ST Express 566 runs north on SR 167 to Kent, Renton, Bellevue and Overlake, and 578 links Puyallup and Seattle. King County Metro 180, 181 and 186 serve Green River College, Enumclaw, Federal Way, Kent and Sea-Tac Airport.
Link light rail at Federal Way
Federal Way Downtown station became the southern end of the Link 1 Line on December 6, 2025, about 16 minutes to SeaTac/Airport and about 56 minutes to Westlake in downtown Seattle.
A City-owned airport two miles north of downtown, with one 3,842-foot runway and no scheduled airline service. In 2019, 264 aircraft were based there.

chapters.title: Parks and outdoors
chapters.intro: The City’s Parks Department manages nearly 1,000 acres of park land, including 33 developed parks, with river access along the Green and White rivers.
items: 20.86 acres at 910 9th Street SE, home to the Auburn Community & Event Center, the Senior Activity Center, the library and the White River Valley Museum. It also has the Discovery Playground and a summer spray playground.
At 3030 R Street SE: 53 acres plus 86.17 acres of open space, with 2 soccer fields, 4 softball fields, a one-mile paved loop trail and the Len Chapman Amphitheater.
At 2401 Stuck River Drive SE, with river access, trails, camping, a picnic shelter and a free 18-hole disc golf course. A pedestrian bridge crosses the White River.
At 413 Western Avenue NW, a wetland park with an elevated boardwalk trail, interpretive signs and a bird-viewing tower.
At 2033 4th Street SE, with swimming and tubing access to the Green River, public fishing access and trail access.
Auburn’s portion of the regional Interurban Trail is 4.5 miles long.
At 402 Mountain View Drive, with a sculpture and views of Mount Rainier and the Auburn valley.
A full-service 18-hole, par 71 course at 29630 Green River Road SE, just over 6,450 yards.

chapters.title: Schools
chapters.intro: Most of Auburn is in the Auburn School District, with parts of northern Auburn in the Kent or Federal Way districts and the Pierce County part listed under Dieringer. Boundaries change; confirm school assignment with the district for any specific address.
items: Serves 17,125 K–12 students across a 62-mile area in parts of King and Pierce counties, including Auburn, Algona, Pacific and Lake Tapps. It has 16 elementary schools, 4 middle schools and 4 high schools.
Auburn High School, Auburn Riverside High School and Auburn Mountainview High School, plus West Auburn High School.
Cascade, Mt. Baker, Olympic and Rainier middle schools.
Portions of northern Auburn are served by the Federal Way and Kent school districts, and the Pierce County portion by the Dieringer School District.
Based in Lake Tapps, it lists three schools: Dieringer Heights Elementary, Lake Tapps Elementary and North Tapps Middle School.
The Auburn School District posts attendance area maps on its website, along with a bus stop finder.
A public community college whose main campus is on Lea Hill, with satellite campuses in downtown Auburn, Enumclaw and Kent.

chapters.title: Everyday errands
chapters.intro: Downtown and the Les Gove Park campus hold the library, museum and Sunday market, with the hospital near the station.
items: The King County Library System’s Auburn Library opened in Les Gove Park in 2000 and was expanded to 20,000 square feet in 2012.
MultiCare Auburn Medical Center at 202 North Division Street has a 24-hour emergency department with Level III trauma designation.
Valley Regional Fire Authority provides fire and emergency medical services to Auburn, Algona and Pacific, with headquarters and Station 31 at 1101 D Street NE.
The City of Auburn provides water, sewer, storm drainage and garbage, recycling and yard and food waste services, depending on address. Waste Management is the listed garbage hauler.
The 2025 Auburn Farmers Market ran Sundays, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., at Les Gove Park, 1140 Auburn Way South, through September 14.
The Outlet Collection Seattle, formerly the SuperMall of the Great Northwest, opened in 1995.

At 918 H Street SE, covering local history, Northwest Indian culture, Japanese-American history and the Northern Pacific Railroad. Exhibits include the 1924 Auburn Depot and a 1915 Japanese farmhouse.

chapters.title: Housing and neighborhoods
chapters.intro: Auburn grew from a downtown hops and railroad town into the surrounding hills, mostly through annexations since the late 1990s.
items: Owner-occupied housing rate 60.6%, median owner-occupied home value $547,900 and median gross rent $1,786 (Census, 2020–2024).
The city lists Downtown, North Auburn, River’s Bend, Christopher/Thomas, Lea Hill, Hazelwood, West Valley, West Hill, South Auburn, Terminal Park, Forest Villa, Lakeland Hills and Hidden Valley.
Auburn annexed West Hill and Lea Hill in 2008, adding 15,000 residents and expanding its land area by 26%.
A master-planned community at the city’s southern end, on both sides of the King–Pierce county line. Construction began in 1985; by 2007 it had 3,600 homes.
On January 1, 2024, Auburn annexed the 155-acre Bridges neighborhood from Kent.
Founded as Slaughter in 1891 and renamed in 1893 after Auburn, New York, a town that also relied on hops farming.

chapters.title: What’s nearby
chapters.intro: Auburn sits between Kent to the north, Federal Way to the west, Algona and Pacific to the south and the Muckleshoot Indian Reservation to the south and southeast.
items: A south King County city of 136,588 people in 2020, with its own Sounder station and the 6,500-seat accesso ShoWare Center. SR 167 crosses the Green River from Auburn into downtown Kent.
West of Auburn’s West Hill. Federal Way Downtown station is the southern end of the Link 1 Line, with 13 bus bays and a five-story garage.
Bordered by Auburn to the north and east and by Pacific to the south, with 3,290 people in 2020. It incorporated in 1955.
Mostly in King County with a part in Pierce County, with 7,235 people in 2020. The lower White River runs through its east side, between Auburn and Sumner.
In northern Pierce County, south of Auburn, with 10,621 people in 2020 and a Sounder stop downtown.
A Thoroughbred racetrack about half a mile east of SR 167, opened in 1996, with live racing in spring and summer. The Muckleshoot Indian Tribe bought the land in 2002.
